87: She is still with her dying friend, and still the same bright, beautiful creature whose presence softens pain and sheds happiness whichever way she turns.
She went out yesterday with her little sisters; I knew of it, went to meet them, and we walked together.
After about an hour and a half we came back toward the town.
We stopped at the spring I am so fond of, which is now a thousand times dearer to me than ever.
Charlotte sat down on the low wall, and we gathered around her.
I looked about me and remembered the time when my heart was still free and unoccupied.
"Since that time I have not come to rest by your cool stream; I have passed you with careless steps, and hardly given you a glance."
I looked down and saw Charlotte's little sister, Jane, coming up the steps with a glass of water.
I turned toward Charlotte, and felt how completely she governs me.
Just then Jane came up with the glass.
Her sister, Marianne, wanted to take it from her.
"No!" cried the child, with the sweetest look on her face.
88: The affection and simplicity of it charmed me so much that I tried to express what I felt by catching the child up and kissing her heartily.
She was frightened and began to cry.
"You should not do that," said Charlotte.
"Come, Jane," she went on, taking her hand and leading her down the steps again, "it does not matter: wash yourself quickly in the fresh water."
The little dear rubbed her cheeks with her wet hands, in the full belief that all the impurities she had caught from my ugly beard would be washed off by that miraculous water.
And though Charlotte said it would do, she went on scrubbing with all her might, as though too much were better than too little.
I assure you, Wilhelm, I have never attended a baptism with greater reverence.
And when Charlotte came up from the well, I could have thrown myself down before her as before the prophet of an Eastern nation.
89: In the evening I could not resist telling the story to a man who, I thought, had some natural feeling, since he was a man of understanding.
But what a mistake I made.
He insisted it was very wrong of Charlotte; that we should not deceive children; that such things give rise to countless errors and superstitions, from which we are bound to protect the young.
It struck me then that this very man had been baptised only a week before.
So I said nothing further, and kept to the justice of my own convictions.
We should deal with children as God deals with us: we are happiest under the influence of innocent delusions.
91: What a child a man is, that he should care so much about a look!
What a child a man is!
We had been to Walheim; the ladies went in a carriage.
During our walk I thought I saw something in Charlotte's dark eyes — I am a fool, but forgive me!
You should see them — those eyes.
However, to be brief, since my own eyes are weighed down with sleep: when the ladies stepped into their carriage again, young W., Seldstadt, Andran and I were standing about the door.
They are a merry set of fellows, all laughing and joking together.
They wandered from one to another; but they never lit on me — on me, who stood there motionless and saw nothing but her!
My heart said goodbye to her a thousand times, and she never noticed me.
The carriage drove off, and my eyes filled with tears.
I looked after her, and suddenly I saw Charlotte's bonnet lean out of the window; she turned to look back — was it at me?
My dear friend, I do not know; and in that uncertainty I find my consolation.
Perhaps she turned to look at me.
Good night — what a child I am!
93: You should see how foolish I look in company when her name is mentioned — especially when someone asks me plainly how I like her.
What sort of creature must a man be who merely liked Charlotte, whose whole heart and senses were not entirely taken up with her?
Someone asked me lately how I liked Ossian.
95: I pray for her recovery, because Charlotte shares my distress.
I see her now and then at my friend's house, and today she told me the strangest thing.
Old M— is a covetous, miserly fellow who has long worried and vexed the poor lady badly; but she has borne her afflictions patiently.
A few days ago, when the physician told us there was no hope of her recovery, she sent for her husband — Charlotte was present — and spoke to him like this:
"I have something to confess which, after my death, may cause trouble and confusion."
"I have managed your household as frugally and economically as I could, but you must forgive me for having defrauded you for thirty years."
"At the beginning of our married life you allowed a small sum for the wants of the kitchen and the other household expenses."
"When our establishment grew and our property increased, I could not persuade you to raise the weekly allowance in proportion."
"In short, you know that when our wants were greatest you required me to provide everything on seven florins a week."
"I took the money from you without a word, and made up the weekly deficiency out of the money-chest — since nobody would suspect your wife of robbing the household bank."
"But I have wasted nothing, and I would have been content to meet my eternal Judge without this confession, except for one thing."
"The woman who takes over the management of your household after my death must not be embarrassed by your insisting that what was allowed to me, your former wife, was enough."
96: I talked with Charlotte about the inconceivable way men let themselves be blinded.
How could anyone fail to suspect some deception, when only seven florins were allowed to cover expenses twice as great?
But I have myself known people who believed, without the least visible astonishment, that their house held the prophet's never-failing cruse of oil.
98: In her dark eyes I read a genuine interest in me and in what becomes of me.
Yes, I feel it; and I may believe my own heart, which tells me — dare I say it? dare I speak the divine words? — that she loves me!
99: How the thought raises me in my own eyes!
And since you can understand my feelings, I may tell you how I honour myself now that she loves me.
100: Is this presumption, or is it a sense of the truth?
I do not know any man who could take my place in Charlotte's heart.
And yet, when she speaks of her betrothed with so much warmth and affection, I feel like a soldier stripped of his honours and titles and robbed of his sword.
102: How my heart beats when I touch her finger by accident, or our feet meet under the table!
I draw back as if from a furnace; but a secret force drives me forward again, and my senses swim.
Her innocent, unconscious heart never knows what agony these little familiarities cost me.
Sometimes, while we are talking, she lays her hand on mine, and in the eagerness of the conversation comes closer to me, and her sweet breath reaches my lips.
Then I feel as though lightning had struck me, and as if I could sink into the earth.
And yet, Wilhelm, with all this heavenly trust — if I know myself, and should ever dare — you understand me.
No, no! My heart is not so corrupt.
It is weak, weak enough — but is that not a degree of corruption?
103: She is a sacred being to me.
All passion falls still in her presence.
I cannot describe what I feel when I am near her.
It is as though my soul beat in every nerve of my body.
There is a melody she plays on the piano with angelic skill — so simple, and yet so full of spirit.
It is her favourite air; and at the first note, all my pain and care and sorrow vanish in a moment.
104: I believe every word that is said about the magic of ancient music.
How her simple song enchants me!
Sometimes, when I am ready to take my own life, she plays that air.
And instantly the gloom and the madness hanging over me are scattered, and I breathe freely again.
106: Wilhelm, what is the world to our hearts without love?
What is a magic lantern without light?
You have only to kindle the flame inside, and the brightest figures shine on the white wall.
And if love shows us nothing but fleeting shadows, we are happy all the same, when we stand before them like children and are carried away by the splendid phantoms.
I have not been able to see Charlotte today.
I was kept by company I could not get free of.
I sent my servant to her house, so that I might at least see somebody today who had been near her.
Oh, the impatience with which I waited for him to come back!
The joy with which I welcomed him!
I would certainly have caught him in my arms and kissed him, if I had not been ashamed.
107: They say that the Bonona stone, laid in the sun, draws in the rays and shines for a time in the dark.
So it was with me and this servant.

The thought that Charlotte's eyes had rested on his face, his cheek, his very clothes, made all of it precious to me beyond reckoning, so that at that moment I would not have parted with him for a thousand crowns.
His presence made me so happy!
Beware of laughing at me, Wilhelm.
Can a thing be a delusion if it makes us happy?
109: That is what I say with delight when I get up in the morning and look out with a glad heart at the bright, beautiful sun.
And then I have no other wish to make: everything, everything is contained in that one thought.
111: I cannot agree to your proposal that I should go with the ambassador to ———.
I do not like being under orders, and we all know that he is a rough, disagreeable man to be attached to.
You say my mother wishes me to be employed.
I could not help laughing at that.
Am I not employed enough already?
And is it not really all one whether I shell peas or count lentils?
The world runs on from one folly to the next.
And the man who toils after gold or honour or any other phantom, purely out of regard for other people's opinion and with no wish or need of his own, is nothing better than a fool.
113: You insist so much on my not neglecting my drawing that I would do better to say nothing at all than to confess how little I have done lately.
114: I have never felt happier, never understood nature better, down to the smallest stem and the least blade of grass.
And yet I am unable to express myself.
My powers of execution are so weak; everything seems to swim and float before me, so that I cannot make a clear, bold outline.
But I fancy I should do better if I had some clay or wax to model with.
If this state of mind lasts much longer I shall try it, and take to modelling — even if all I knead is dough.
115: I have begun Charlotte's portrait three times, and three times disgraced myself.
It is the more annoying because I used to be very successful at taking likenesses.
I have sketched her profile since, and must content myself with that.
117: I will order and arrange everything.
Only give me more commissions, the more the better.
One thing I must ask, though: use no more writing-sand on the dear notes you send me.
Today I raised your letter hastily to my lips, and it set my teeth on edge.
119: I have often resolved not to see her so often.
But who could keep such a resolution?
Every day I meet the temptation, and promise faithfully that tomorrow I will really stay away.
But when tomorrow comes, I find some irresistible reason to see her; and before I can account for it, I am with her again.
Either she has said the evening before, "You will be sure to call tomorrow" — and who could stay away after that?
Or she gives me some commission, and I find it essential to bring her the answer in person.
Or the day is fine, and I walk out to Walheim; and once I am there, it is only half a league further to her.
I am inside the charmed circle, and soon find myself at her side.
My grandmother used to tell us a story about a mountain of loadstone.
When any ship came near it, it was stripped of its ironwork in an instant: the nails flew to the mountain, and the unhappy crew perished among the falling planks.
121: Albert has arrived, and I must take my departure.
Were he the best and noblest of men, and I his inferior in every respect, I could not endure to see him in possession of such a perfect creature.
Possession! Enough, Wilhelm: her betrothed is here — a fine, worthy fellow whom one cannot help liking.
Fortunately I was not present at their meeting.
It would have broken my heart!
And he is so considerate: he has not given Charlotte a single kiss in my presence.
I have to love him for the respect with which he treats her.
He shows a regard for me; but I suspect I owe that more to Charlotte than to any liking of his own.
Women have a delicate tact in such matters, and so they should.
They cannot always manage to keep two rivals on good terms with each other; but when they do, they are the only ones who gain by it.
122: The coolness of his temper stands out strongly against the impetuosity of mine, which I cannot conceal.
He has a great deal of feeling, and knows perfectly well what a treasure he has in Charlotte.
He is free of ill humour — which, as you know, is the fault I detest most.
123: He takes me for a man of sense; and my attachment to Charlotte, and the interest I take in everything that concerns her, add to his triumph and his love.
I shall not ask whether he may not sometimes tease her with small jealousies.
I know that in his place I should not be entirely free of such feelings myself.
124: But be that as it may, my pleasure with Charlotte is over.
Call it folly or infatuation — what does a name matter?
Before Albert came I knew everything I know now.
I knew I could make no claim on her, and I made none — that is, as far as it is possible not to long for such loveliness when it stands in front of you.
And now here I am like a silly fellow, staring in astonishment when another man walks in and takes my love away.
125: I bite my lips and feel an infinite scorn for the people who tell me to be resigned, since there is no help for it.
Let me escape from the yoke of such silly subterfuges!
And when I come back to Charlotte and find Albert sitting beside her in the summer-house in the garden, I cannot bear it: I behave like a fool and commit a thousand extravagances.
"For Heaven's sake," Charlotte said today, "let us have no more scenes like those of last night!"
"You terrify me when you are so violent."
Between ourselves, I am always away now when he visits her; and I am delighted when I find her alone.
